candidate_relations.reason: Temperature was 36.6 degrees Celsius after the dive, with no clinical evidence of hypothermia.
Blood pressure of 90/60 mm Hg documents hypotension, but it does not explain post-ascent arthralgia and right-heart microbubbles.
The patient had acute movement-related arthralgia without erythema or swelling, making joint pain a manifestation rather than primary arthritis.
Symptoms began after rapid ascent and before therapeutic high-flow oxygen, so oxygen toxicity does not fit the sequence.
Nitrogen narcosis occurs under pressure at depth, whereas this syndrome followed rapid ascent and included circulating microbubbles.
There was no trauma or fracture and echocardiography visualized gas microbubbles rather than evidence of fat emboli.
Dyspnea and arterial PO2 of 63 mm Hg show hypoxia secondary to the decompression illness.
The exposure was a sea-depth dive and chest radiography was normal without pulmonary edema.
Right-sided microbubbles after ascent are related to diving gas injury, but no patent foramen ovale or focal arterial neurologic syndrome was demonstrated.
The afebrile patient had no wound, tissue infection, or radiographic gas to support gas gangrene.
The precipitating event was decompression from 50 m and there was no carbon monoxide exposure history.
Dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia indicate respiratory compromise, but the normal chest study and post-dive bubbles identify the underlying decompression disorder.
The patient rapidly ascended from underwater rather than traveling to high altitude.
Rapid ascent from a 50 m saturation dive followed by severe arthralgia, confusion, dyspnea, and intracardiac microbubbles is diagnostic of decompression sickness.
Mild confusion supports cerebral involvement, but the prominent generalized arthralgia and hypoxemia show a broader multisystem decompression illness.

candidate_relations.reason: There was no oxidant exposure or characteristic persistent saturation discrepancy to suggest methemoglobinemia.
The white-cell count of 13 × 10^9/L is a secondary laboratory abnormality rather than the post-ascent diagnosis.
Oxygen saturation of 90% and PO2 of 63 mm Hg document hypoxemia as part of the decompression presentation.
A normal D-dimer, normal echocardiographic right-heart function, and directly seen microbubbles after ascent favor decompression sickness over pulmonary embolism.
Acute generalized joint pain without swelling or erythema arose immediately in the decompression setting rather than from an independent arthritic condition.
